title: Compilers and optimization levels (-O2, LTO, inlining)
summary: What -O0 to -O3 really switch on, why inlining and vectorization drive most speedups, how LTO and ThinLTO optimize across files, and what PGO, -march and fast-math cost.
outcomes: Explain why -O0 code keeps every variable in memory and what bundles -O1, -O2, -O3, -Os, -Og and -Ofast enable
Trace how inlining enables constant folding, and why it cannot cross .c files without LTO
Predict whether GCC vectorizes a loop at -O2 or -O3 given its trip count and pointer aliasing
Compare monolithic LTO with ThinLTO and use -flto correctly at compile and link time
Choose PGO, -march and -ffast-math knowing what each one risks

blocks.md:
You compile the same C file twice, once with `-O0` and once with `-O2`, and one binary runs several times faster. Nothing in your algorithm changed. What changed is how much freedom you gave the compiler to rewrite your program, as long as the visible result stays the same.

This course is about that freedom: what the levels turn on, the three transformations that matter most (**inlining**, **vectorization**, **link-time optimization**), and the flags that buy speed at a price.

Start with the default. The GCC manual says that without optimization the goal is fast compiles and predictable debugging: *statements are independent*, so you can stop at a breakpoint, change any variable, and the program continues exactly as the source says. To make that true, the compiler keeps every variable in its stack slot and reloads it at each statement.

blocks.caption: We compile this with GCC 14 for x86-64 Linux and print Intel-syntax assembly with -S -masm=intel.

blocks.title: The same loop at -O0 and at -O2 (x86-64, GCC)
blocks.code:
; gcc -O0 (Intel syntax)
sum:
  push rbp
  mov  rbp, rsp
  mov  QWORD PTR [rbp-24], rdi   ; a to stack
  mov  QWORD PTR [rbp-32], rsi   ; n to stack
  mov  QWORD PTR [rbp-8], 0      ; s = 0
  mov  QWORD PTR [rbp-16], 0     ; i = 0
  jmp  .L2
.L3:
  mov  rax, QWORD PTR [rbp-16]   ; load i
  lea  rdx, [0+rax*8]
  mov  rax, QWORD PTR [rbp-24]   ; load a
  add  rax, rdx
  mov  rax, QWORD PTR [rax]      ; load a[i]
  add  QWORD PTR [rbp-8], rax    ; s += (load+store)
  add  QWORD PTR [rbp-16], 1     ; i++ (load+store)
.L2:
  mov  rax, QWORD PTR [rbp-16]   ; load i
  cmp  rax, QWORD PTR [rbp-32]   ; load n
  jl   .L3
  mov  rax, QWORD PTR [rbp-8]
  pop  rbp
  ret
; gcc -O2
sum:
  test rsi, rsi                  ; n <= 0?
  jle  .L4
  lea  rdx, [rdi+rsi*8]          ; end = a + n
  xor  eax, eax                  ; s = 0 (in rax)
.L3:
  add  rax, QWORD PTR [rdi]      ; s += *p
  add  rdi, 8                    ; p++
  cmp  rdi, rdx
  jne  .L3
  ret
.L4:
  xor  eax, eax
  ret

scenes.caption: At -O0 the first thing sum does is copy its arguments a and n from registers into stack slots, and give s and i stack slots too. Every variable now lives in memory.
One trip through the -O0 loop: 10 instructions, 7 memory loads and 2 stores, to do one addition. i and s are reloaded from memory every time because the compiler keeps each statement independent.
At -O2, s stays in register rax and the index is replaced by a pointer that walks the array. The loop is 4 instructions with a single load.
For n = 1000 that is 10013 instructions at -O0 versus 4005 at -O2. Nothing about the algorithm changed, only how much the compiler was allowed to assume.

blocks.md: An **optimization level** is not one magic switch. It is a named bundle of individual passes, each with its own `-f` flag: `-ftree-dce` (dead code elimination), `-finline-small-functions`, `-ftree-loop-vectorize` and so on. Each level turns on everything the previous one did plus more. Run `gcc -Q --help=optimizers -O2` to print the exact set your GCC build enables, since it varies a little by target.

blocks.title: How the GCC optimization levels relate

scenes.caption: -O0 is the default. GCC disables most optimization passes here, even ones you request with -f flags, so that the code matches the source line by line.
-O1, -O2 and -O3 are cumulative bundles. The GCC manual lists 48 flags for -O1, 54 more for -O2 and 12 more for -O3 (counted from the current manual).
-O2 is the usual release level: nearly every optimization without a space-speed tradeoff. -O3 adds loop transforms and a more willing vectorizer.
Side branches: -Og is -O1 minus passes that hurt debugging, -Os is -O2 minus passes that grow code, and -Oz trades even more speed for bytes.
-Ofast is -O3 plus -ffast-math and other options that are not valid for every standards-conforming program. It can change your results.

blocks.md:
The variants, as the GCC manual defines them:

- `-O1` (same as `-O`): cheap optimizations that do not take a lot of compile time.
- `-O2`: nearly all optimizations that do not trade space for speed.
- `-O3`: adds loop transforms such as `-funswitch-loops`, `-fpeel-loops` and a vectorizer cost model that accepts runtime checks.
- `-Os` and `-Oz`: optimize for size. `-Og`: optimize but keep the debugging experience.
- `-Ofast`: `-O3` plus `-ffast-math` and other rule-bending options.

Clang accepts the same spellings with similar meanings.

blocks.title: sum(a, 1000) compiled at each level (x86-64, GCC)

scenes.caption: Instructions executed for n = 1000, counted from each listing. -O3 wins because it vectorizes the loop (lesson 3); -Os executes more than -O2 because it chose a smaller loop shape.
Size of the sum function in bytes. -O3 is 3x bigger than -O2 (setup and cleanup code around the vector loop) and -Os is the smallest. Speed and size pull in different directions.

blocks.prompt: You compile with `gcc -O2 -O0 file.c` because a Makefile appends flags. Which level is used?
blocks.reveal: **-O0.** The GCC manual says that with multiple `-O` options the *last* one wins. This is a classic reason a benchmark build is mysteriously slow: some later variable in the build system appended `-O0` or `-Og`. Check the actual compile command, not the one you think you wrote.

blocks.md: Misconception: "-O3 is always faster than -O2." -O3 makes code bigger and adds transforms that only pay off for some loops. Bigger code can cost instruction-cache misses. Measure both on your workload; -O2 is the common default for release builds.

An -O level is a bundle of passes. -O0 keeps every variable in memory for debuggability; -O2 is the standard speed level; -O3, -Os, -Og and -Ofast each trade something (size, speed, debuggability, strictness) for something else.

blocks.question: In the -O0 listing, why does the loop reload `i` from the stack every iteration even though it just stored it?
options: The CPU requires a load before every add
The -O0 contract keeps statements independent so a debugger can change i between them
The register file is too small to hold i
-O0 does not know how to use registers at all
blocks.explain: At -O0 GCC promises that stopping between statements and editing a variable works as the source says. So each statement reads its inputs from memory and writes results back. Registers are used, but only briefly within one statement.

blocks.question: You ship firmware into a 32 KB flash chip and the hot path is not performance critical. Which level fits best?
options: -Ofast
-Os or -Oz
blocks.explain: -Os enables the -O2 passes except those that often grow code, and -Oz goes further. In the measured sum function -Os produced 22 bytes versus 35 at -O2 and 105 at -O3. -O0 is both big and slow.

lessons.title: Inlining: removing a call unlocks every other optimization

blocks.md:
A function call has a direct cost: move arguments into registers as the ABI requires, execute `call` and `ret`, and set up and tear down a stack frame. For a tiny function that overhead can exceed the work itself.

The bigger cost is indirect. Most optimizations look at one function body at a time. Across a call boundary the compiler knows little about the callee, so it must assume the worst: the arguments could be anything and the callee might read or write memory.

**Inlining** replaces a call with a copy of the callee's body, with the parameters substituted by the actual arguments. The GCC manual puts it this way: besides removing call overhead, "if any of the actual argument values are constant, their known values may permit simplifications at compile time". Inlining is cheap by itself; its value is that it hands the next passes a bigger body with more facts in it.

blocks.code:
static int square(int x) { return x * x; }
int f(void) { return square(7) + 1; }
blocks.caption: Compiled at -O0 and at -O2 with GCC for x86-64.

blocks.title: Inlining square(7), then folding the constant

nodes.label:
static int square(int x)
return x * x;

scenes.caption: At -O0 f really calls square: it moves 7 into edi (the first argument register), executes call, and square sets up its own stack frame. 7 + 7 instructions to compute a constant.
Step 1, inline: the compiler copies square's body into f with x replaced by 7. The call, the argument move and square's frame setup all disappear.
Step 2, constant folding: 7 * 7 + 1 is known at compile time, so it becomes 50. This step was impossible before inlining because the compiler optimizes one function body at a time.
Final -O2 output: mov eax, 50 then ret. square was static and every call was inlined, so GCC does not emit it at all.

blocks.md:
Which calls get inlined is a heuristic decision, controlled by flags the levels turn on:

- `-finline-functions-called-once` (from -O1, not -Og): a `static` function with one call site is merged into its caller.
- `-finline-small-functions` (-O2): inline when the body is smaller than the call sequence, so code shrinks.
- `-finline-functions` (-O2, also enabled by `-fprofile-use`): consider every function and let a size and benefit estimate decide.

If all calls to a `static` function are inlined, no standalone copy is emitted.

The tradeoff is code size. Each inlined call site gets its own copy of the body. Inline a 40-instruction function at 50 call sites and you added about 2000 instructions, which can push hot code out of the instruction cache. The GCC manual says the effect of inlining on size "is less predictable": it may shrink or grow the program. This is one reason `-Os`, which tunes decisions for code size, inlines very differently from `-O3`.

Misconception: the `inline` keyword forces inlining. It is a hint plus linkage rules. At -O2 the compiler inlines functions you never marked, and may refuse ones you did. At -O0 GCC inlines nothing unless the function has `__attribute__((always_inline))`.

blocks.prompt: Now move `square` into its own file `sq.c` (not static), keep only the declaration `int square(int x);` in the file with `f`, and compile each file with `gcc -O2 -c`. What does `f` compile to?
blocks.reveal:
A real call:

`sub rsp, 8` / `mov edi, 7` / `call square` / `add rsp, 8` / `add eax, 1` / `ret`

The compiler sees one **translation unit** (one .c file after preprocessing) at a time. When it compiles f, square is only a declaration with no body, so there is nothing to inline and 50 cannot be computed. Lesson 4 fixes this with link-time optimization.

blocks.md: You can ask the compiler what it decided. GCC prints optimization remarks with `-fopt-info-inline` and Clang with `-Rpass=inline` (successes) or `-Rpass-missed=inline` (refusals). Reading these is faster than guessing from the assembly.

Inlining matters less for the call it removes than for what it enables: constant folding, dead code removal and vectorization inside the merged body. It costs code size, and it only works when the callee's body is visible in the same compilation.

blocks.question: A hot loop calls `int clamp(int v)` defined in another .c file. Profiling shows the call overhead dominates. You compile with -O3. What happens?
options: -O3 inlines it because -O3 enables aggressive inlining
It stays a call: the body is in a different translation unit
It is inlined only if clamp is marked inline in its own .c file
The linker inlines it automatically
blocks.explain: Inlining needs the callee's body. Without LTO each .c file is compiled alone, so no -O level can inline across files. Moving clamp into a header as static inline, or using -flto, makes the body visible.

blocks.question: Why can inlining make a program slower even though it removes call instructions?
options: Inlined code cannot be vectorized
It always disables constant folding
Duplicated bodies grow the code and can cause instruction-cache misses
Inlined functions run at -O0
blocks.explain: Every call site gets its own copy. For large functions with many call sites, the bigger hot path may no longer fit in the instruction cache, and those misses can cost more than the calls saved. Compilers use size budgets for this reason.

lessons.title: Vectorization and why -O2 and -O3 differ on loops

blocks.md:
Modern CPUs have **SIMD** (single instruction, multiple data) registers. On x86-64 the 128-bit `xmm` registers hold four 32-bit ints, and one `paddd` instruction adds four pairs at once. SSE2, which provides them, is part of the baseline x86-64 target, so every x86-64 binary may use it.

**Auto-vectorization** is the compiler rewriting a scalar loop so each iteration processes several elements in SIMD lanes.

blocks.caption: Two versions of the same loop. restrict promises the compiler that the three arrays do not overlap.

blocks.title: a[i] = b[i] + c[i]: scalar steps versus 4-lane SIMD steps

scenes.caption: Scalar code (-O1): one load, one add and one store per element. Iteration 0 computes 3 + 2 = 5.
Iteration 1: 1 + 7 = 8. Eight elements need eight trips through the loop.
Vectorized (-O2 here): movdqu loads 16 bytes, that is four ints, from b and from c; paddd adds all four pairs in one instruction; movups stores four results.
Second vector iteration covers elements 4 to 7. Two trips instead of eight. For 1024 elements the loop runs 256 times instead of 1024.

blocks.code:
add_1024:            ; gcc -O2, x86-64
  xor  eax, eax
.L11:
  movdqu xmm0, XMMWORD PTR [rsi+rax]  ; 4 ints of b
  movdqu xmm1, XMMWORD PTR [rdx+rax]  ; 4 ints of c
  paddd  xmm0, xmm1                   ; 4 adds
  movups XMMWORD PTR [rdi+rax], xmm0  ; 4 ints of a
  add  rax, 16
  cmp  rax, 4096                      ; 1024 ints x 4 bytes
  jne  .L11
  ret
blocks.caption: The real vector loop GCC emits: 7 instructions per 4 elements.

blocks.md:
Vectorizing is only legal if it gives the same result as the scalar loop. Two things get in the way:

1. **Unknown trip count.** If n is not a multiple of 4, a scalar **epilogue** loop must finish the last 1 to 3 elements.
2. **Possible aliasing.** If `a` overlaps `b` or `c`, a store in one iteration can change what a later iteration reads. Then the compiler must add a **runtime check** and keep a scalar fallback, which is called *versioning* the loop.

blocks.prompt: Call the plain `add` with `b = {1,1,1,1,1}`, `c = {1,1,1,1}`, `a = b + 1` (so a[i] is b[i+1]) and n = 4. What does b hold after the scalar loop, and what would a naive 4-lane vector version produce?
blocks.reveal:
Scalar: each store feeds the next load. b[1] = 1 + 1 = 2, then b[2] = b[1] + 1 = 3, and so on, giving **b = {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}**.

Naive vector: it loads b[0..3] = {1,1,1,1} *before* storing anything, adds 1, and writes {2,2,2,2}, giving **b = {1, 2, 2, 2, 2}**. Different answer, so the transformation is illegal for this overlap. GCC's -O3 code for `add` checks the pointer distance first and takes the scalar path when a starts 1 to 3 ints after b or c; a == b (in place) is safe and stays vectorized.

blocks.md:
This is where -O2 and -O3 differ. GCC's -O2 enables the vectorizer with `-fvect-cost-model=very-cheap`, which refuses any loop that needs a runtime alias or alignment check. In GCC 12 to 14 it also required the vector loop to replace the scalar loop entirely, so a loop with an unknown trip count (which needs a scalar epilogue) was refused; [GCC 15](https://gcc.gnu.org/gcc-15/changes.html) relaxed this and accepts unknown trip counts. -O3 switches to the `dynamic` model, which accepts runtime checks and epilogues. Compiling the examples with GCC 14 (`-fopt-info-vec` prints each decision):

- `add` (unknown n, no restrict): -O2 not vectorized; -O3 vectorized and "versioned for vectorization because of possible aliasing".
- `add_1024` (fixed count, restrict): vectorized at -O2.

Clang's loop vectorizer is on by default at -O2 and adds runtime pointer checks itself.

blocks.title: Instructions executed, counted from GCC's x86-64 output

scenes.caption: add_1024 (restrict pointers, 1024 ints): scalar -O1 executes 6146 instructions; -O2 and -O3 both vectorize it with SSE2 and execute 1794.

sum(a, 1000) with unknown n: GCC 14 at -O2 refuses to vectorize because it would need a scalar epilogue for an odd n, so only -O3 gets the 2-lane version: 4005 versus 2519. GCC 15 and 16 still leave it scalar at -O2.

blocks.md: `restrict` is a promise, not a check. If you mark pointers restrict and then pass overlapping arrays, the behavior is undefined and the vectorized loop can silently compute the wrong answer shown above.

Vectorization processes several elements per instruction, but only when the compiler can prove it is safe: known trip counts and non-overlapping pointers help. -O2 in GCC vectorizes only the easy cases (no runtime checks, and before GCC 15 no epilogue); -O3 also takes loops that need runtime alias checks.

blocks.question: A loop over `float *out, const float *in` with a runtime length n is not vectorized at `gcc -O2` but is at -O3. What is the most likely reason?
options: -O2 does not support SIMD instructions
-O2's very-cheap cost model rejects loops that need a runtime alias check
Floats can never be vectorized at -O2
The loop needs -march=native first
blocks.explain: With runtime n and two pointers that may overlap, vectorizing needs a runtime overlap check. The very-cheap model used at -O2 refuses any runtime alias check (and, before GCC 15, any loop needing a scalar epilogue); -O3's dynamic model accepts them. restrict (plus a known trip count on GCC 14 and older) can make -O2 vectorize it.

blocks.question: Why does adding `restrict` to all three pointers let the compiler drop the runtime check?
options: restrict makes the arrays aligned to 16 bytes
restrict tells the compiler the arrays do not overlap, so stores cannot affect later loads
restrict forces -O3
restrict copies the arrays before the loop
blocks.explain: The check exists only to detect overlap. restrict promises there is none, so the compiler can vectorize unconditionally. If the promise is false the program has undefined behavior.

lessons.title: LTO and ThinLTO: optimizing across source files

blocks.md:
Lesson 2 showed a call the compiler could not inline because the callee lived in another .c file. That is the normal state of a C program: each file is compiled alone into a .o, and the linker only glues machine code together. No interprocedural optimization crosses a file boundary.

**Link-time optimization (LTO)** moves the optimizer to link time, when every file is available.

blocks.code:
# without LTO
gcc -O2 -c sq.c -o sq.o
gcc -O2 -c main2.c -o main2.o
gcc -O2 sq.o main2.o -o nolto

# with LTO: -flto and -O2 at compile AND link time
gcc -O2 -flto -c sq.c -o sq.o
gcc -O2 -flto -c main2.c -o main2.o
gcc -O2 -flto sq.o main2.o -o lto
blocks.caption: The square example split into two files. main2.c has int main(void) { return f(); } with f calling square(7) + 1.

blocks.prompt: Disassemble `main` in both binaries (`objdump -d`). The non-LTO main is `sub rsp, 8; mov edi, 7; call square; add rsp, 8; add eax, 1; ret`. What does the LTO main look like?
blocks.reveal: Two instructions: `mov eax, 0x32` then `ret`. 0x32 is 50. At link time GCC saw both bodies, inlined square into f and f into main, and folded the constant, exactly as in lesson 2. `nm` on the LTO binary no longer lists `square` or `f` at all.

blocks.title: GCC link-time optimization in WHOPR mode

nodes.label:
WPA: whole call graph
inline + partition

scenes.caption: Compile step (LGEN, parallel per file): with -flto, GCC writes its internal representation GIMPLE into special ELF sections of each .o instead of, or as well as, machine code.

Link step: the GCC driver sees LTO sections and runs lto1. WPA (whole program analysis) reads the call graph and summaries of every file and makes global decisions, such as inlining square from bar.o into main in foo.o.
WPA is sequential. It splits the program into partitions of roughly equal size, minimizing references that cross between them, and writes them out with its decisions.
LTRANS runs the partitions in parallel, applies the decisions and generates machine code. The linker then produces the final binary as usual.

blocks.md:
Some practical rules from the GCC manual:

- Pass `-flto` and the same `-O` options at compile time **and** at link time. An `-O` given only at link time is largely ineffective, because early passes and the summaries they produce run at compile time.
- LTO objects are *slim* by default (GIMPLE only), so `ar` and `nm` must understand them; use `gcc-ar` and `gcc-nm`, or `-ffat-lto-objects` to also store normal machine code.
- With fat objects a misconfigured build silently links the machine code and LTO is quietly skipped.

LLVM's full (monolithic) LTO merges the whole program into one module in one compiler process, which costs a lot of memory and time for big programs and redoes everything after any edit. GCC's default WHOPR mode above already runs LTRANS in parallel, but its WPA step still reads the whole program. LLVM's **ThinLTO** keeps the cross-module benefits without that. Per the Clang docs, each compile emits bitcode plus a compact **summary**. The link step reads only the summaries, merges them into a combined index, and decides which functions each module should import. The modules are then optimized in fully parallel backends, by default one thread per core. A cache lets incremental builds skip unchanged modules. Usage: `clang -flto=thin -O2` at compile and link.

blocks.title: Monolithic LTO versus ThinLTO on 4 modules (toy model)

scenes.caption: Simplified model: compiling each file takes 2 units and optimizing each module takes 2. Monolithic LTO merges all modules into one and optimizes it on one core: 2 + 4 x 2 = 10 units, and all of it repeats after any edit.

ThinLTO: each compile also writes a small summary. A fast serial thin link merges only summaries (1 unit), then four backends optimize in parallel, each importing the few functions it needs (assumed 0.5 extra): 2 + 1 + 2.5 = 5.5 units.
Incremental rebuild after editing m2 with the ThinLTO cache on: only m2 recompiles, the thin link reruns, and only backends whose inputs changed rerun (here m2 alone); the rest come from the cache.

blocks.md: LTO can expose latent bugs. Code with undefined behavior, or with mismatched declarations of the same function in different files, may have "worked" only because the optimizer could not see across files. When LTO breaks a program, suspect the program first.

Without LTO, a .c file is the optimizer's horizon. LTO stores the compiler's IR in the object files and optimizes the whole program at link time. ThinLTO does the global analysis on small summaries and the heavy work in parallel, so it scales and supports incremental builds.

blocks.question: A teammate adds `-flto` only to the final link command; all .o files were compiled without it. What happens?
options: Full LTO across all files
No cross-file optimization: the .o files contain only machine code
The link fails
Only main.c is re-optimized
blocks.explain: LTO works on the IR stored in object files. Objects compiled without -flto contain only machine code, so the link-time optimizer has nothing to work with. -flto (and -O) must be given at compile time too.

blocks.question: Which part of a ThinLTO build is serial?
options: Compiling each source file
The thin link that merges summaries and decides imports
Optimizing each module's backend
Writing the final object files
blocks.explain: Compiles and backends run in parallel. Only the thin link is serial, and it is fast because it reads compact summaries rather than whole function bodies.

blocks.question: Why does monolithic LTO hurt the edit-compile-test loop on a large project?
options: It disables -O2
It cannot run on multicore machines at all
Any edit forces re-optimizing the single merged module of the whole program
It requires profile data
blocks.explain: Monolithic LTO merges every module into one and optimizes it as a unit, so a one-line change redoes the expensive whole-program step. ThinLTO's cache re-runs only the backends whose inputs changed.

lessons.title: PGO, -march=native and -ffast-math: speed with strings attached

blocks.md: The compiler guesses a lot: which branch of an `if` is likely, which call is hot, how many times a loop runs. **Profile-guided optimization (PGO)** replaces the guesses with measurements from real runs. The Clang manual's examples: knowing a branch is taken very often improves the ordering of basic blocks, and knowing which functions are called often helps the inliner.

scenes.caption: Step 1: build an instrumented binary. It contains counters on branches and calls.
Step 2: run it on representative inputs. On exit GCC's runtime writes a .gcda file per object; Clang writes .profraw files that llvm-profdata merge converts into one .profdata.
Step 3: rebuild with the profile. The compiler now knows which branches are hot, which calls are frequent and how many times loops iterate, and lays out and inlines accordingly.

blocks.md: In GCC, `-fprofile-use` also turns on optimizations that are usually only profitable with a profile, including `-funroll-loops`, `-fpeel-loops`, `-ftracer` and `-fvpt`. GCC reports an error by default when the profile no longer matches the source. Clang can also use **sampling** profiles from a profiler such as perf, via `-fprofile-sample-use`, which avoids the instrumented build at the cost of less precise counts.

PGO optimizes for the inputs you profiled. The Clang manual warns that code not exercised in the profile "will be optimized as if it is unimportant". Profiling only a unit-test suite or a single toy input can make the real workload slower.

Second lever: the target instruction set. By default x86-64 compilers target a generic CPU with SSE2. `-march=native` enables every instruction set extension of the machine doing the compiling, and the GCC manual warns that the result "might not run on different machines". The x86-64 psABI (the processor-specific ABI standard) defines portable middle steps: `-march=x86-64-v2`, `x86-64-v3` (which adds AVX2) and `x86-64-v4`.

blocks.title: add_1024: instructions executed by target ISA (GCC)

scenes.caption: Baseline x86-64 has 128-bit SSE2 vectors: 4 ints per add, 256 iterations, 1794 instructions.
With -march=x86-64-v3 GCC uses 256-bit ymm registers and vpaddd: 8 ints per add, 128 iterations, 771 instructions. Fewer instructions, but the binary now requires AVX2.

blocks.md: Third lever: floating-point rules. IEEE arithmetic is not associative, so $(a+b)+c$ can differ from $a+(b+c)$. A float sum loop therefore cannot be split into vector lanes without changing results, and GCC's -O3 leaves it scalar. `-ffast-math` sets `-fno-math-errno`, `-funsafe-math-optimizations` (which includes `-fassociative-math`), `-ffinite-math-only` and more. No -O level enables it except `-Ofast`.

blocks.title: Summing 8 floats: source order versus 4 vector lanes

scenes.caption: Source order: s = 0 + 1e8, then + 1. In 32-bit float the gap between neighbours near 1e8 is 8, so 1e8 + 1 rounds back to 1e8.
All three 1s are lost, then -1e8 brings the sum to 0, and the last three 1s survive: the strict IEEE answer is 3. This is what -O2 must produce.
With -ffast-math the compiler may reassociate into 4 lanes: lane k sums x[k] + x[k+4], giving 0, 2, 2, 2, then adds the lanes: 6. Clang -O2 printed 3; -O2 -ffast-math printed 6.

blocks.md: -ffast-math assumes no NaNs or infinities (-ffinite-math-only), so code that relies on IEEE behavior of NaNs and infinities can give incorrect results. Clang has deprecated -Ofast because an optimization flag changing the observable behavior of correct code surprises people. Enable fast-math per file or per function when you have verified the numerics, not globally.

Benchmark fairly: compare builds that differ in one flag, print the real compile command, and confirm what changed with `-fopt-info-vec` (GCC), `-Rpass=loop-vectorize` (Clang) or the assembly from `-S`. A speedup you cannot explain from the generated code is often a measurement error.
PGO, -march and fast-math can each beat any -O level, but each adds a condition: representative profiles, a known target CPU, and numerics that tolerate reordering.

blocks.question: You build a CLI tool on a new workstation with `-O2 -march=native` and publish the binary for all Linux x86-64 users. What is the main risk?
options: It runs slower on older CPUs
It may use instructions older CPUs lack, so it fails to run there
It produces different numeric results on AMD
Nothing, -march only affects scheduling
blocks.explain: -march=native enables every extension of the build machine, and the GCC manual warns the result might not run elsewhere. For a distributed binary use the default target, a psABI level like x86-64-v2 or v3 that you document, or runtime dispatch. -mtune changes scheduling only.

blocks.question: A physics simulation's results change in the 6th digit after switching from -O3 to -Ofast. What is the most likely cause?
options: -Ofast has a compiler bug
-Ofast enables -ffast-math, which allows reassociating floating-point operations
-Ofast uses less precise 16-bit floats
-Ofast disables vectorization
blocks.explain: -Ofast is -O3 plus -ffast-math. Reassociation (for example splitting a sum into vector lanes) changes rounding, exactly as in the 8-float example where the result went from 3 to 6. Neither answer is a bug; the strict one is what the source specifies.

blocks.question: You collect a PGO profile by running only the test suite, which mostly exercises error paths. What is likely to happen on production traffic?
options: Production gets the full PGO speedup anyway
The hot production paths may be treated as cold and optimized for size or laid out poorly
The compiler refuses the profile
The binary crashes on untested paths
blocks.explain: PGO trusts the counts. Paths the profile never saw look cold, so they may be laid out away from hot code and inlined less. Profile with inputs that represent the real workload.
